thread_title: S. leucophylla RED clone A x B select clone, Franklin Co, FL
breadcrumb: S. leucophylla RED clone A x B select clone, Franklin Co, FL

posts.body_html:
Aside from what I've seen in the wild, the reddest S. leucophylla I've ever seen in cultivation is S. leucophylla clone B Franklin Co, FL. I believe that clone originally came from sunbelle. Anyhow, I got this select clone below from my good homie Rob Co of the pitcher plant project (BTW, he's famous and was recently published in sunset magazine!) It's a cross between two red clones from the franklin Co, FL population: clone A x clone B. I've seen other seedlings from this batch, and they don't compare to this plant, which is vigorous, and just an absolute beauty.

Another nice thing about this clone is that it produced a decent crop of spring pitchers. However, the most impressive, darkest red traps are produced in the fall. These traps will turn even darker red and perhaps could turn the entire trap solid red during the winter dormancy period, but that is still yet to be seen (I just got this plant last winter).

S. leucophylla clone A x clone B 'select clone' Franklin Co, FL. Photos were taken 9/28/13:












Even the developing new pitcher is bright red:

posts.body_html:
Looks great, Mike! These Franklin County leucos from the western edge of 'Tate's Hell' tend towards large, and as you stated, they produce really nice spring pitchers. We have a tray of seedlings, only a month old, coming along where we crossed Franklin County "B" and "D" onto "C". All three clones are reds from the same stand, so we look forward to seeing what the percentage break-down will be on these in terms of coloration. BTW, we had excellent germination and the babies are looking strong.
Kiwiearl, like you stated, we believe in breeding true to location, and wish we had more locations to work with. This particular stand in Franklin County is gone now.

Oct 11, 2013 13:27:35 GMT -5 sunbelle said:

Kiwiearl, like you stated, we believe in breeding true to location, and wish we had more locations to work with. This particular stand in Franklin County is gone now.


The work you and guys like Mike are doing is invaluable. The results will be really interesting.

Sometimes the whole thing feels a bit like the captive animal breeding programmes where there are greater numbers of a species/subspecies in captivity than in the wild. The Amur Leopard, Panthera pardus orientalis, is a great example. A subspecies that is as about as critically endangered as you can get with only ~26 left in their East Asian habitat, numbers of Amurs in captivity conversely are ~200. Its that old dichotomy: keeping animals captive is questionable, but without that the subspecies has almost zero future as an entity. If you've never seen an Amur Leopard before check it out on line. A gorgeous cold adapted cat.

Clearly some wild populations of Sarracenia have little chance as the future ticks over. At least concerted knowledgeable and accurate efforts in cultivation allow for them to remain what they are, even without a home to go to. And that last measure requires so much thought and planning as to be no flash in the pan notion.

posts.body_html: What is interesting about the Franklin County site is the absence of any other Sarracenia species. The nearest flava that we know of are many miles away, and there are no psittacina. We know introgression plays a part in colors and shapes, but perhaps it is over-rated. We think leucophylla can express red color without introgression, as seen in these Franklin County specimens (BTW, there are more traditional colors present as well)which are isolated. We know others who have visited the site and never found other S. species. The last time our friend Manny visited the site, he found Pinguicula planifolia, which was never seen before there.

posts.body_html:
Here's an amusing anecdotal story: For the last week or so, with cooler nights (finally below 26 degrees C /80 degrees F), I like to sit outside amid the Sarrs just after sunset, sipping on a brew. Part of the experience includes an interesting dusk visitor: three large moths that visit the leucophyllas, hovering like hummingbirds, lapping up the sugary droplets on the lid and around the lip. They never stop hovering, moving from pitcher to pitcher. One interesting thing I noticed: they never visit other Sarracenia--strictly staying with leucos. I saw one moth buzz around a (leuco x moorei), but no deal. It went straight for the nearby Purple Lip x self! Hybrids are not acceptable, even when it's three fourths leuco. Talk about choosy! The moths have no problem with our red leucos from Franklin County, indicating that there is no hybrid introgression. I trust the moths more than some human experts.

With a wink and a smile,
Trent
